messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Carl is a 60-year-old warehouse worker who lives with his partner of thirty years in a small Midwestern town. He came to therapy at her urging, after months of escalating withdrawal and what she described as a “darkness” that had settled over him. The trauma that haunts Carl occurred during his military service, forty years ago, when he was a young soldier in a convoy ambushed in a narrow, dusty ravine. He remembers the heat, the smell of diesel and blood, and the moment the truck in front of him hit an IED. He watched his closest friend, a man named Reyes, die instantly, while Carl—shocked but physically unharmed—was pulled from the wreckage. For decades, he told himself it was just part of the job, something to bury and move past. But in the last few years, the memories have refused to stay buried.

When Carl tries to recall that day, he often finds himself stuck, unable to find the right words to describe what he saw or felt. He knows the facts, but the language to explain the terror and the guilt slips away, leaving him frustrated and mute. What does come back, unbidden and vivid, is the raw terror of the explosion—the same visceral fear he felt at that moment, as if he is back in the ravine. Worse than the fear is the guilt that surges with every memory. He has come to believe that he should have died instead of Reyes, that his survival was a mistake, a cosmic error. This belief has hollowed him out. He feels like he no longer knows who he is; the person he was before the ambush—a confident young man with a future—seems like a stranger. In its place is a hollow shell, certain that the world is fundamentally dangerous, that safety is an illusion. This conviction colors everything: a car backfiring on his street makes him drop to a crouch; a sudden loud noise in the warehouse sends his heart racing for hours.

Because he is certain the world is dangerous, Carl has developed a rigid set of strategies to keep himself safe. He avoids driving anywhere near the old military base on the outskirts of town, taking a twenty-minute detour that makes his commute absurdly long. At work, he refuses to wear the navy-blue coveralls required by the warehouse, because they remind him of the uniform he wore that day. He told his supervisor he had a skin allergy, and now he wears old, loose-fitting clothes that violate the dress code, earning him repeated warnings. More than anything, he avoids thinking about the event itself. When a memory starts to surface—triggered by a news report about a faraway war, or the sight of a dusty pickup truck that resembles a military vehicle—he forces his mind to go blank, distracting himself with menial tasks or counting objects on the shelves. This avoidance has become a full-time job. His partner has noticed that he no longer watches any movies with action or violence, and he has stopped visiting his brother, who lives near the base. The more he avoids, the more the world shrinks, and the more he feels he has lost his identity. He has begun to feel that his avoidance is proof that he is broken, that the real Carl—the one who could face life—is gone forever.

The memories themselves also drive his avoidance. When the terror of the ambush floods back, he feels an urgent need to escape his own mind. He will leave the dinner table mid-meal, or walk out of the grocery store, abandoning a full cart. He has learned that if he can just stop the memory from completing—by moving, by changing his environment—the guilt and fear will recede, at least temporarily. But the relief is short-lived. Each time he flees, his guilt deepens. He tells himself that he is a coward, that Reyes would have stayed and fought, that he does not deserve to be alive. This self-condemnation makes the next memory even more punishing, because it arrives already layered with shame. The cycle tightens: a memory triggers avoidance, avoidance confirms his guilt, and guilt makes the next memory more vivid and terrifying.

In the warehouse, the most difficult moments come when he has to unload a truck from a dusty loading dock. The smell of dry dirt and exhaust can send him reeling. He has started requesting the quietest, most isolated shifts—the overnight inventory count—where he can work alone, in silence, with minimal triggers. His supervisor has noticed his declining reliability and has written him up twice for leaving his station without explanation. Carl knows his job is at risk, but he cannot explain why he flees. What frightens him most is the growing sense that he is disappearing. He came to therapy because his partner told him she was afraid to come home to a man who sometimes seems not to be there at all. Carl is afraid of the same thing. He is terrified that if he lets himself remember fully, he will drown in the guilt. But he is equally terrified that the avoidance is erasing him, piece by piece.
